title: Reward Top K Students
statement:
The arrays `positive_feedback` and `negative_feedback` list praising words and critical words; no word is in both. There are `n` feedback reports: `report[i]` is a sentence of lowercase words separated by single spaces, written about the student whose ID is `student_id[i]`. Every student ID is distinct, so each student has exactly one report.

A student starts at 0 points. Every word of their report that equals a praising word adds 3 points, and every word that equals a critical word subtracts 1 point (a word that appears several times counts each time; other words change nothing).

Rank the students by points from highest to lowest, placing the smaller ID first when points are equal, and return the IDs of the first `k` students of this ranking, in ranking order.
constraints: positive_feedback[i] and negative_feedback[j] contain only lowercase English letters
No word appears in both positive_feedback and negative_feedback
report[i] contains only lowercase English letters and spaces, with exactly one space between consecutive words
signature: List<Integer> topStudents(String[] positive_feedback, String[] negative_feedback, String[] report, int[] student_id, int k)

notes:
## Intuition

Scoring a report means asking, for each of its words, "is this a praising word? a critical word?". Searching the feedback lists every time would cost their full length per word; putting both lists into hash sets makes each question O(1). After every student has a score, the ranking is just a sort with a two-part key: points descending, then ID ascending.

## Approach

1. Build the sets `positive` and `negative` from the two feedback lists.
2. For each report `i`, split it on spaces and start `points` at 0: add 3 for a word in `positive`, subtract 1 for a word in `negative`.
3. Store the pair `[points, student_id[i]]` in `students`.
4. Sort `students` by points from high to low, breaking ties by the smaller ID.
5. Return the IDs of the first `k` entries.

## Example 1, step by step

`"this student is studious"`: only `"studious"` is in `positive`, so student 1 gets 3 points. `"the student is smart"`: `"smart"` is praising, so student 2 also gets 3. Both have 3 points, so the smaller ID comes first, and the answer is `[1, 2]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(P + N + W + n log n): building the sets, splitting all reports (W words), and sorting the `n` students; P and N are the total feedback lengths.
- Space: O(P + N + n) for the sets and the `students` list.

## Pitfalls

- Match whole words only: `"smartest"` is not `"smart"`, so test the split words against the sets instead of searching the sentence for substrings.
- A word repeated in a report counts every time it appears.
- Scores can be negative; the comparator must still put higher points first and only then compare IDs.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `positive`, `negative` | hash sets of praising and critical words |
| `students` | `[points, id]` pairs, one per report |
| `points` | the score of the report being read |
| `word` | one word of that report |

narration.3: Do the same for the critical words.

narration.15: Remember the student's final points together with their ID.

narration.19: Keep the first k students of the ranking and return their IDs.
